title: FIFA's Credibility Crisis Overshadows a Riveting World Cup as Integrity Questions Mount Before Final
excerpt: From Cristiano Ronaldo's paused suspension to a Trump phone call that lifted a US player's ban, FIFA faces a growing backlash over political interference and officiating controversies heading into Sunday's Argentina-Spain final.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Cristiano Ronaldo's suspension was paused, allowing him to play in Portugal's opening matches.
  • FIFA's inclusivity promise failed, with strict US visa policies blocking fans from several countries.
  • Over 7 million abusive posts were detected during the tournament, a 14-fold increase from 2022.
  • Officiating controversies raised questions about FIFA's integrity and favoritism towards marketable stars.
FIFA's Integrity Under Fire
›Cristiano Ronaldo's suspension paused for group-stage matches.
›Folarin Balogun's ban lifted after Trump's call to FIFA.
›Controversial officiating decisions raised integrity concerns.
›FIFA denied political influence, but skepticism remains.
  • FIFA paused Cristiano Ronaldo's suspension so he could play in Portugal's opening games, and lifted US striker Folarin Balogun's automatic ban after President Trump called FIFA President Gianni Infantino.
  • The Sport & Rights Alliance says FIFA's promise of the "most inclusive" World Cup has "largely failed," citing strict US visa policies that shut out fans from Morocco, Egypt, Jordan and other nations.
  • FIFA's Social Media Protection Service detected more than 7 million abusive posts targeting players and officials during the tournament — 14 times higher than the 2022 edition.
  • Officiating controversies in Argentina's knockout-round matches have fueled perceptions that FIFA tilted the competition toward its most marketable stars.

A Tournament Defined by Two Interventions

As Argentina and Spain prepare to meet in Sunday's World Cup final, the conversation around the 2026 tournament has shifted from what happened on the pitch to what happened behind the scenes. Two decisions by FIFA have come to define the event's legacy — and neither involved a ball.

The first came before the tournament opened, when FIFA paused a suspension against Cristiano Ronaldo, allowing the Portuguese star to play in his team's opening two group-stage matches. The second occurred mid-tournament, when US striker Folarin Balogun had his automatic one-game ban effectively removed after President Donald Trump placed a call to FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

FIFA strenuously denied that Trump's call influenced the decision, but few observers believed the denial. The episode backfired on the Americans, who were eliminated in the round of 16 by Belgium.

"That FIFA had so clearly put its thumb on the scale in those two instances, tossing aside the integrity of the competition in the process, only increased the scrutiny on the officiating controversies that arose in the World Cup's later stages."

— theScore

Officiating Under the Microscope

The Ronaldo and Balogun episodes opened the door to broader scrutiny. When Switzerland scored to level their quarterfinal against Argentina at 1-1, Swiss striker Breel Embolo was sent off minutes later after a second yellow card issued through VAR's "mistaken identity" rule — a procedure never before used in a World Cup.

Combined with favorable calls in Argentina's comeback against Egypt, the pattern led neutrals to question whether FIFA was giving breaks to Lionel Messi in what is likely his final World Cup. Analysts noted that while a direct pro-Messi directive from Infantino to match officials was implausible, FIFA's willingness to bend its own rules in the Ronaldo and Balogun cases made it impossible to extend the benefit of the doubt.

Visa Policies Undercut Inclusivity Promise

Off the field, the tournament's promise of inclusivity collided with US immigration policy. The Sport & Rights Alliance, a coalition of human rights organizations, said Thursday that FIFA's pledge to welcome the world had "largely failed."

Fans from Morocco, Egypt, Jordan, Iraq and Uzbekistan struggled to obtain US visas despite holding valid tickets. A Somali World Cup referee, Omar Abdulkadir Artan, was barred from entering the United States despite a valid visa, with the Trump administration citing links to "suspected members of terror organisations." Several countries, including Senegal, were grossly underrepresented in stadium crowds after the US suspended visa issuance to most of their citizens.

"The claim that FIFA has made welcome to the world, unite the world to the World Cup has largely failed," said Ronan Evain, executive director of Football Supporters Europe.

Record Online Abuse

FIFA's Social Media Protection Service reported detecting more than 7 million potentially harmful or abusive posts targeting players, coaches and officials during the tournament — a 14-fold increase from the 470,000 detected at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. The team reviewed over half a million AI-detected messages and reported more than 1,000 threats to law enforcement. Racial abuse accounted for 11 percent of detected offensive content.

What It Means for 2030

The integrity questions carry implications well beyond Sunday's final. The Sport & Rights Alliance plans to release a comprehensive report in September detailing human rights issues at the tournament. For FIFA, which awarded the 2030 World Cup to a six-nation bid spanning Morocco, Spain, Portugal, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, the 2026 edition has become a cautionary case study in how political entanglement and operational shortcuts can overshadow brilliant football.

"This World Cup has had much to celebrate," said Minky Worden of Human Rights Watch. "But the dark side of policies by the tournament's principal hosts has also been inescapable."
